blocks.p: This is the second part of my Shutdown Experiences Survey results. Here I'll share how far away safety feels for someone who's in shutdown, how long people have been in shutdown, how long an episode of shutdown lasts, and the actual words of the people in shutdown about what it's like. Get ready to receive some validation and normalization. You are not alone in your shutdown experiences.

The general experience of shutdown is disconnection: from yourself, from the environment, and from others. Part of this disconnection is numbness, physical numbness and emotional numbness. Part of it could be actual dissociation: being cut off from yourself, feeling like you're not in your body, or feeling like reality isn't real.

Both of these have to do with the safety state. If you don't have access to your safety state, it results in defense. That could be flight, or fight, or shutdown, or freeze. You have to have access to your safety state in order to feel connected.
Shutdown is the furthest rung down the Polyvagal ladder, so it's the furthest away from the safety state.

blocks.h: How far away safety feels, and where to start

blocks.p: So how far away does safety feel from shutdown? There were five options to pick from. Here's each one, with what I'd focus on from there.

blocks.h3: "I can't even see my safety state from here"

blocks.p: This was the highest, at 42 percent. That sounds like a significant amount of shutdown. The safety state seems completely unreachable from this deep shutdown experience. These people probably don't even know how to access their safety state. That's pretty common for someone in shutdown: not knowing how to feel or experience what's within them, and that includes their safety state. Someone who can't even see their safety state is probably in a pretty hopeless, helpless, unmotivated kind of state.

Where to start: sensory safety cues might be the most accessible. Connecting to yourself, recognizing your emotions, or connecting to other people might be too much to ask. Using your senses in a lower stimulation environment might be the most accessible way to feel some safety, or some grounding in the present moment. I highly recommend reduced stimulation, and working on increasing your passive safety cues.

blocks.h3: "I see it, it's possible to get there, but I don't know how"

blocks.p: This was about 12 percent. This person has touched on some safety in the past, and they still have the capacity for it, but it's a pretty big challenge.

Where to start: it might be best to focus on sensory safety, but also memory and imagination. Imagination and memory are functionally pretty much the same thing when it comes to anchoring in safety. A memory might help you focus on a specific experience of safety from the past, so it might be an accessible way to experience safety again now, even while existing in shutdown. Imagination plays a similar role, but it's something you have to create with your mind.

blocks.h3: "I touch into my safety state every now and then, but I lose it easily"

blocks.p: About 22 percent said this, and it's a pretty common sentiment. I think a lot of the people who come to my courses and community, and to my content, are in this boat. They have an experience of safety, and maybe they can do something on purpose to feel more safety in their system, but they can't hold on to it. They know there's something there they can actively work toward, and things that just feel better, but they lose it really easily. I think this is common not just in shutdown, but in any defensive state.

To me this indicates you're building self-regulation. Something is going right with your safety state, and maybe even with building your vagal brake. The safety state is strengthening. It's accessible, but it's hard to hold on to, which is a pretty normal part of change and trauma recovery, or any self-development really.

Where to start: start with, or solidify, the passive safety cues in your environment, then mindfully use more active means. Set up your safety environment at home with things that generally feel better than not. Then actively do other things: yoga, meditation, using your senses, movement. There are a lot of options. Do those things mindfully. Really experience them in your safety environment. That might help get you to the next step.

blocks.h3: "I feel safety often, but I'm still in shutdown often too"

blocks.p: This was also at 22 percent, and that's completely okay.

Where to go from here: keep focusing on safety. Eventually the immobilization of shutdown, plus safety, will turn into stillness. Stillness is the ability to not move and be okay with it. Stillness results in more mindfulness. It results in meditative practices. It results in being able to go to sleep. Stillness is huge, and we do it all the time. I'm being still right now in this chair as I record this. So shutdown might eventually turn into stillness if you practice safety enough and really deepen your anchoring in your safety state.

And from that deep enough safety anchoring, and from stillness, can come mobilization. If you can immerse yourself in a shutdown that is deeply connected to safety, your self-regulation might take the next step and climb up the Polyvagal ladder into fight and then flight. You might notice some mobilization coming into your system. That's a really good sign. Stay anchored in your safety state and allow that mobilization to come as it does.

Deb Dana described that climb when she was on the podcast: "To begin to leave dorsal, you have to travel through sympathetic... we have to have our energy used in an organized way and often in connection with somebody else." ([Episode 29](https://player.captivate.fm/episode/f8b9643c-28f8-4185-9525-8b4e6301516c))

blocks.h3: "I have lots of access to my safety state. I experience shutdown as stillness."

blocks.p: Only one person selected this. Congratulations to that one person. Whatever you're doing, keep it up.

blocks.why: This article talks about anchoring in safety. This practice does just that, tuned to you.

blocks.h: How long people have been in shutdown

blocks.p: The next question was how long have you been in shutdown? As a therapist, a coach, and someone who gets messages from listeners all the time, I know how long people can exist in shutdown, or any defensive state. So the results weren't a surprise to me. But I also know that people are surprised when they hear they've been in shutdown for a long time and that they're not alone. It's super common to be in a shutdown state, or really any other defensive state, for a very long time, even decades.

Childhood always plays a role in our current states: the way we were parented, our upbringing, our neighborhoods, our companions growing up. All of these affected us for better or worse. I know it sounds like a very therapy-ish thing to say, but it's true. Our nervous system adapts based on the needs of the context, the needs of survival. If you needed to exist in a shutdown state to get your needs met, or to get through the day, or to get through the moment, over and over, then your nervous system likely developed in a more shutdown state.
Here's what people said:

ul: The highest, 24 percent, said they'd been in shutdown for one to three years. Three to four years before this survey was the COVID pandemic lockdown, forced isolation pretty much globally. I tend to think that has something to do with it. If I had done the same survey in 2020, with the COVID quarantines, the civil unrest, and a very intense election in the USA, I assume the number of people in shutdown would have been higher.
18 percent said they'd been in shutdown within the past year.
3 percent, two people, said 41 to 50 years.
Seven people, 10 percent, said they'd been in shutdown for over 50 years.

blocks.p: Shutdown can exist for a long, long time. For the people who've been in shutdown for over 50 years, think about the attitudes about mental health back then. What was the attitude about speaking up about your emotions, or seeking help, 50 years ago? What did their families teach them? Were they taught to recognize and express all of their emotions, or just some of them? Or to repress them, to keep quiet for the family, or for whatever group they were part of?

One of my community members said during one of our meetups that to be a "good little girl" meant not expressing yourself when you were young. A couple of the women in my group have said something very similar.

blocks.h: How long an episode of shutdown lasts

blocks.p: The next question was how long does an acute episode of shutdown last? In other words, when is shutdown dominant, without enough safety in your system? In the survey I used the language "periods where shutdown is obvious or more intense than usual."

ul: The most common answer was less than a day, at about 21 percent. This person is probably isolating, probably not wanting to get out of bed, having negative thoughts, maybe even thoughts about death, but they're probably mostly functional. The shutdown is definitely noticeable, though.
14 percent said less than a week.
20 percent said between one and four weeks.
5 percent said one to two months.
Almost 12 percent said shutdown never ends.

blocks.p: That's a big range for how long shutdown can last.

blocks.h: What can help an acute shutdown

blocks.p: So what could help you come out of an acute shutdown? Listen to what your body needs, and mindfully provide it.

From the first part of the survey, we know that someone in shutdown needs lower stimulation, and kind of needs to be alone. So doom scrolling is not going to help. Binging on things is not going to help. Substances don't really help. You might feel less shut down doing these things, but they don't help you come out of shutdown or recover from it. They just mask the problem.

If you can, mindfully experience the underlying emotions and sensations of shutdown. That's very difficult. It might be terrifying to think about. That's why the priority is always to anchor in safety first. If you can be in safety, then you can mindfully experience the emotions that come from shutdown. That's what I mean by mindfully. As long as you're existing in safety, the intensity of those emotions might soften, and some self-regulation out of shutdown might occur.

Mindfully experiencing your shutdown might mean that if you need to cry, you let yourself cry. That might even mean a lot of crying. Crying does not mean you're weak. It does not mean you're failing. It might just be part of the process. If you need to cry more the next day, then you cry more the next day. People who have a lot of crying to do often judge themselves. They call themselves weak. They say they're failing. They don't just accept that they have a real feeling and that it needs to be released, and crying is often how it's released.
Regardless of all this, the priority must be safety:

ol: Identify what safety feels like for you.
Identify what helps you get to safety.

blocks.p: I'll finish with the words of the people who took the survey, describing their experiences of shutdown. I tried to whittle these down, but it's hard when there are so many great descriptive words that I think you need to hear if you're in shutdown. It helps to hear that you're not alone, that other people experience something similar to you. It can validate you, normalize you, and give you new language.
They're grouped by how long each person has been in shutdown. They're not easy to read, but I didn't feel it was right to water them down or censor them. There are no trauma descriptions.

blocks.h3: In shutdown within the past year

blocks.p: One person wrote: "It's like staring into the abyss."
Another: "My body feels heavy, gray, zombie like."
Another:

q: Everything feels too much and too overwhelming, while at the same time there is huge amounts of apathy and just not caring about anything. I want to run away and have zero responsibility. I become all consumed with thoughts about me and my suffering and nothing else matters.

blocks.h3: In shutdown for one to three years

blocks.p: One person wrote: "Exhausted like I'm filled with lead or have been drained of blood."
Another:

q: Nothing can be done. Not one thing will fix this. And I am correct in this. Except, time passes, and one morning, one day, maybe I stick my neck out.

blocks.p: Another:

q: Devoid of hope, nothing will ever change, feel completely stuck in the state. It feels like a force pulling you down, and you no longer have the strength to fight it, so you just give in to it.

blocks.p: Another: "Like a heavy wall is blocking my view of reality, but I can't see past it and I can't move it."

blocks.h3: In shutdown for four to ten years

blocks.p: One person wrote:

q: I barely feel my body at all, instead just feeling the need to crawl into a dark and silent corner to disappear. Thoughts are tumbling over each other, but in such a disconnected and foggy way that I can't grab them.

blocks.p: Another:

q: There are varying degrees. Very intense shutdown feels as if my body is very heavy. All I want to do is go to bed and lie in the dark. My thoughts are quite dark and hopeless, or I feel very unreal, as if I'm not really here. I daydream a lot, and this is my most common coping mechanism when I'm in an intense state of shutdown. It's the only thing that stops me from crying, to disappear in my head into a fantasy story that I make up.

blocks.p: Another: "Shutdown is like I've sunken into the depths of the ocean."
Another:

q: Like falling down a big black bottomless hole, but it's not necessarily uncomfortable. The isolation warms the air around me. Darkness becomes my bodyguard. As bad as it is, and it is really bad, although I have never considered any form of suicide or self harm, neither am I scared of death either. In short, shutdown to me is a temporary form of death.

blocks.p: One person wrote: "It's a dark cave with no way out."
Another:

q: I'm tired all the time, yet can't manage to sleep at night at all, but somehow I can sleep for hours during the day. I can't accomplish any of my responsibilities, and I don't even want to think about them. I get overstimulated easily by everything around me and have no appetite. I call my kind of shutdown doom spiraling.

blocks.p: Another:

q: It's like trying to see through fog to walk through quicksand. Everything takes concerted effort and takes so much energy there is none left over for connecting with others or even trying to find safety. I am constantly fighting the desperate and all consuming drive to find somewhere dark to hide and shut down or sleep. I genuinely feel like when it's at its most intense I will die if I do not isolate and switch off. I fight it but it's exhausting and struggle to think positively but have faith in the impermanence of the state.

blocks.p: One person wrote:

q: Like being alone in a dark well with no ladder to climb out and no one coming to save me. This is extreme and acute shutdown. On a day to day basis where I dip into shutdown, it often feels like a nausea and sinking feeling in my stomach. Combined with fatigue, lack in motivation and feelings of worthlessness or why am I even bothering?

blocks.p: Another: "Disconnected, like part of me has fallen asleep."
Another: "Waiting to die alone and knowing I deserve it."
One person wrote: "I feel so useless. I hate myself for what I have been through. I wish I had never been born."
Another:

q: My shutdown feels like an out of body experience and I become silent and unresponsive. I feel like I'm losing my identity and uncertain of who I am and why I exist. Often times when in shutdown, I want to sleep forever or hide under blankets.

blocks.p: Another:

q: My life feels visually muted, like looking up through a tumultuous water after a huge wave has clobbered you, disorienting. My life sounds tuned out, not just in a peaceful sense, but more like Charlie Brown's teacher in the Snoopy shows, womp womp, where I can't make out meaning or hear actual words in my environment. Tactilely, my body literally loses its sense of pain. Sensations of extreme hot or cold are numbed, and the natural hunger or thirst drive get turned off.

blocks.p: One person wrote: "Dissociative. Blurry. Not really living. No energy. No drive. With fear as a normal state. Just want to get by."
One person wrote: "I lose myself. I collapse. I cry. I have no voice. Even though I think and feel a great deal."
Another:

q: It's like waiting for my life to happen. Wondering who I am, then feeling like time will run out before I answer those questions. Then I glimpse at the terror of becoming real and go back to shutdown. The moments of shutdown are being inside my own head where I am not even present and nothing around me touches me. It's empty and numb. I'm invisible to others. Everything is flat. No one wants me to come out, and I wouldn't know how if I tried.

blocks.p: And another: "Existing but not living."

Thank you so much to everyone who shared their experiences of shutdown. And for you, reading this, I really hope it gives you some new language, some validation, and some normalization for what you're going through.
